name: Sadegh Hedayat
description: A journey through the life of a disillusioned and lonely intellectual whose dark vision and existential despair opened a new path in the storytelling of his homeland.

ending.title: Your Fate as an Unknown Writer

events.title: Encounter with New Literature
events.playerFact: As a teenager in Tehran, you stumble upon a translated collection of foreign stories—tales full of darkness, mystery, and psychological depth. Something inside you stirs, and you feel these words might describe that deep void you've always carried.
events.historicalFact: In your youth, you were deeply influenced by Western literature, and this influence forever changed your literary path.
events.question: Do you immerse yourself in these translated stories and let them shape your worldview?

yes.consequence: You become fascinated by their dark, psychological atmospheres and begin steering your own notes toward new, bitter themes.

no.consequence: You reject these foreign influences and decide to write strictly within classical Persian forms—ghazals and qasidas.

events.title: Studying Abroad
events.playerFact: Your wealthy family sends you to Europe to study a practical field—engineering, architecture, or dentistry. But in the lecture halls, your mind wanders elsewhere: to crowded writer's cafés and the books you truly long to read.
events.historicalFact: You traveled to Europe for studies, but spent more time writing and exploring modern literary scenes than attending classes.
events.question: Do you continue your formal education and earn a university degree?

yes.consequence: You earn your degree but feel hollow inside—returning home with a diploma in hand and a regret in your heart.

no.consequence: You abandon formal studies and spend your nights in the literary circles of Paris and Brussels, feeding your soul with modernism.

events.title: On the Edge
events.playerFact: Loneliness and existential anguish have become unbearable. One cold afternoon, you find yourself by a dark river in a major European city, contemplating the futility of everything.
events.historicalFact: In the late 1920s, you attempted suicide but were rescued, and after some time, you returned home.
events.question: Do you refrain from attempting suicide and choose to continue living?

yes.consequence: You walk away from the river and vow to fight your inner demons only with pen and paper.

no.consequence: You jump, but a passerby saves you. You survive, but the experience leaves an even deeper scar on your psyche.

events.title: Publishing the First Book
events.playerFact: Back in Tehran, you have notebooks filled with short, pessimistic stories. These writings are unlike anything in the official Persian literary scene—bitter, introspective, and full of doubt. Publishers are afraid, but you want to speak your truth.
events.historicalFact: In 1930, you published your first collection of stories, laying the foundation for modern Persian literature.
events.question: Despite the heavy traditional climate, do you push to have these stories printed?

yes.consequence: Your book is published. It stirs waves of shock and disgust, but you also gain a small group of loyal readers.

no.consequence: You hide the manuscripts in a drawer, take a simple clerical job in a government office, and write only in secret.

events.title: The Obsessive Novella
events.playerFact: For years, you've been working on a long, nightmarish story—a repetitive, hallucinatory tale of a lonely painter haunted by an ethereal, maddening woman. It is your most honest, and yet most horrifying, piece of writing.
events.historicalFact: In the early 1930s, you created your literary masterpiece, which became a symbol of dark, modern Persian fiction.
events.question: Do you finish this maddening story and try to publish it, even knowing it will most likely be banned?

yes.consequence: You complete the story and search for a way to print it, fully aware that it might be confiscated at home.

no.consequence: Fearing scandal and arrest, you burn the entire manuscript and decide never to show it to anyone.

events.title: Publishing Abroad
events.playerFact: Censorship at home has closed all doors. A friend tells you about a small printing press in a neighboring country (India) that might take such a book. You would have to undertake a risky journey.
events.historicalFact: In 1936, you traveled to India, published your masterpiece there, and also developed an interest in ancient Iranian languages and culture.
events.question: Do you endure the hardships of traveling to that distant country to get your book printed?

yes.consequence: You go to India, publish the book, and stay there for months, becoming fascinated with ancient Persian heritage (Pahlavi and Zoroastrian studies).

no.consequence: You cancel the trip, leaving the book to gather dust forever. Your name remains confined to small circles in Tehran.

events.title: The Atmosphere of Oppression
events.playerFact: You've returned, but things are worse. Traditionalists and government agents attack your writings. You stand isolated, yet you cannot stop writing sharp satires and social critiques.
events.historicalFact: Upon returning to Iran, you faced severe censorship and wrote satirical, critical works that further alienated you.
events.question: Do you give up writing and withdraw from society?

yes.consequence: You stop writing altogether, only scribbling private notes for yourself, and withdraw from society.

no.consequence: You continue writing and distributing your work underground, becoming a banned yet influential author.

events.title: The End of the Journey
events.playerFact: Your depression has reached its peak. There is no place left for you in Iran, nor in Europe. You decide to return to that European city of your youth—perhaps for good.
events.historicalFact: In 1951, you returned to Paris and ended your life by gas in a small apartment.
events.question: Do you refrain from suicide and return to Iran instead?

yes.consequence: You resist the temptation of death, return to Iran, and spend the rest of your life in relative peace and obscurity.

no.consequence: You end your life, but years later, your writings are recognized as a treasure of Persian dark literature, and your name becomes immortal.

events.title: The Classicist Poet
events.playerFact: You put aside foreign stories and immerse yourself in the mystical poetry of Rumi and the lyrical ghazals of Hafez. You find safety and peace in classical forms.
events.historicalFact: Some intellectuals of that era, resisting Westernization, turned to reviving pure Persian poetry.
events.question: Do you dedicate all your energy to composing classical ghazals and panegyric odes?

yes.consequence: You become a well-regarded poet in courtly circles and achieve financial security, but slowly feel a sense of stagnation.

no.consequence: You remain undecided between tradition and modernity; your poems are neither pure classical nor relevant modern works, and no one takes you seriously.

events.title: A Comfortable but Empty Life
events.playerFact: Your classical poetry gains a wide following and is recited in aristocratic gatherings. But something gnaws at you—these old forms cannot express the anxieties of the new world.
events.historicalFact: Many traditional poets of that era achieved fame but lacked genuine originality.
events.question: Do you dare to introduce bitter, modern themes into your classical poetry, risking your popularity?

yes.consequence: You try, but not only do you fail—you are ridiculed by both traditionalists and modernists, and you are rejected by both sides.

no.consequence: You stay on the safe path, collecting awards and titles one after another, but deep down, you feel like nothing but a hypocrite.

events.title: Fire and Ashes
events.playerFact: You burned your manuscript. But the obsessive story comes back to life in your nightmares. A year later, you rewrite it from memory, but this time from a fresh perspective.
events.historicalFact: Some writers, after burning their work, later returned to it with regret and rewrote it.
events.question: Do you send the rewritten version to a publisher?

yes.consequence: Under a pseudonym, you send the story to a publisher and this time it receives acclaim. But your identity remains hidden.

no.consequence: You burn the manuscript again, and this time, you give up writing forever.

events.title: The Anonymous Translator
events.playerFact: Under a pseudonym, you begin translating Western literary works—Kafka, Sartre, Camus—into Persian. Your translations are published without your name, but in intellectual circles, everyone knows that the anonymous translator is the one who once wrote that obsessive story.
events.historicalFact: Some intellectuals of that era used pseudonyms to translate and publish modern works.
events.question: Do you reveal your true identity and achieve literary fame?

yes.consequence: You reveal your identity and become known as a pioneering translator, but you never write a new story again. Your name lives on in the history of translation.

no.consequence: You remain anonymous for life, known only to a small circle of friends. When you die, no one knows what a treasure of Western literature you brought into Persian.

events.title: An Outcast of Two Worlds
events.playerFact: Rejected by both traditionalists and modernists, you belong to neither world. You wander aimlessly, a stranger to everyone.
events.historicalFact: Literary history is full of wandering figures who lost their place in the transition from tradition to modernity.
events.question: Do you turn to music and singing to escape this restlessness?

yes.consequence: You meet a Romani musician in Tehran and turn to music. Your soulful voice makes you a beloved singer in night cafés.

no.consequence: You take refuge in Sufism and mysticism. You spend years in khanaqahs (Sufi lodges) in spiritual retreat, eventually becoming known as an intellectual cleric who reached faith through literature.

events.title: The Soulless Court Poet
events.playerFact: You continue on the safe path, becoming a court poet who composes panegyrics for kings and ministers. You are wealthy and respected, but every night you tell yourself that you are nothing but a hypocrite.
events.historicalFact: Some poets of that era gained wealth by flattering the court, but lost their artistic integrity.
events.question: In middle age, do you grow tired of this inauthentic life and search for another truth?

yes.consequence: You abandon everything overnight and travel. You spend years in India and Pakistan, eventually returning to Iran as a scholar of Eastern religions.

no.consequence: You remain the soulless court poet until the end. You die wealthy, but your name appears only in the margins of literary history among the imitators.

events.title: Reflection of a Lifetime
events.playerFact: In old age, you look back at all the paths you've taken. Each road you chose left a mark of you on it. Now it is time to reflect.
events.historicalFact: Every human being, at the end of life, faces the question: 'Was what I did worth it?'
events.question: Are you satisfied with the entire journey of your life?

yes.consequence: You die with peace of mind, knowing that even if you never achieved global fame, you lived honestly and never betrayed yourself.

no.consequence: You die regretting all the paths you never took, wishing you had walked one of them with more courage.

events.title: The Night Café Singer
events.playerFact: With your soulful voice, you become a beloved singer in the cafés of Tehran and Paris. Your songs tell stories of loneliness and the beauty of life. Your stage name is on everyone's lips.
events.historicalFact: Some intellectuals of that era turned to music as a new way to express their feelings.
events.question: Do you go to Paris to continue singing in its famous cafés?

yes.consequence: You go to Paris and become an international singer. You live in Europe for years, and your name shines alongside the greats of café music.

no.consequence: You stay in Tehran and turn to traditional Persian music. You become known as a singer of classical radif, performing in private aristocratic gatherings.

events.title: The Intellectual Cleric
events.playerFact: After years of retreat in Sufi lodges, studying mystical texts, you have arrived at a new understanding of faith. You are now known as an intellectual cleric who bridges tradition and modernity.
events.historicalFact: Some intellectuals of that era, by turning to mysticism, reached a new interpretation of religion.
events.question: Do you return to Tehran to teach comparative mysticism?

yes.consequence: You return to Tehran and become a university professor. Your courses on comparative mysticism attract many students, and your name is recorded as an influential figure in the philosophy of religion.

no.consequence: You stay in the lodge and spend the rest of your life in meditation and writing mystical treatises. Your works gain attention in mystical circles after your death.

events.title: Life on the Margins
events.playerFact: You return to Iran and start a simple life in a quiet corner of Tehran. You have stopped writing and spend most of your time reading and walking. Few people know that you are the author who once caused such controversy.
events.historicalFact: Some disillusioned writers, after years, turned to simple, anonymous lives.
events.question: In this simple life, do you find peace?

yes.consequence: You live with deep peace and, in the end, become known among small circles of friends as a wise elder who withdrew from the world.

no.consequence: The regret of your vibrant past stays with you until the end. Every night, memories of Paris and unfinished writings pass through your mind.

events.title: Immortality Through Death
events.playerFact: You end your life. But in the years that follow, your writings are recognized as a treasure of Persian dark literature. Your name becomes immortal in the history of Persian literature, and future generations know you as a pioneer of modernism.
events.historicalFact: Sadegh Hedayat committed suicide in Paris in 1951, and after his death, he became one of Iran's most influential writers.
events.question: In your final moments, were you aware of this posthumous immortality?

yes.consequence: In your last moments, with the awareness that your works will live on after you, you find peace. Your death becomes a rebirth for Persian literature.

no.consequence: You die believing that everything ends with you. But the world you leave behind is far greater than what you imagined in those final moments.
